newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia praises Iraq, favours more oil sales.
newsitem.headline: Russia praises Iraq, favours more oil sales.

text.p: Russia praised Iraq on Friday for cooperating with the United Nations on disarmament and said Baghdad should be allowed to sell more oil to buy food for its struggling population.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov also urged Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz at a meeting in Moscow to step up efforts to clarify the fate of Kuwaiti citizens who went missing during Baghdad's invasion in 1990.

"It was noted with satisfaction that Iraq is commited to a constructive cooperation with the U.N. Special Commission and a prompt clarification of the outstanding questions which could open the way to lifting the oil embargo against Iraq," the Russian foreign ministry said in a statement.
Aziz, keen to drum up world support for the lifting of sanctions imposed by the United Nations after the invasion of Kuwait, briefly visited Moscow on his way home from a trip to China.
U.N. sanctions bar Baghdad's oil exports until the U.N. Special Commission -- the body in charge of disarming Iraq -- testifies that it has no more weapons of mass destruction.
But the U.N. in December allowed Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food and medicine.

"Taking into account the grave humanitarian situation in Iraq, the sides stressed the need to prolong the U.N. Security Council resolution 986 and increase Iraq's export quotas for oil," the statement said.

Resolution 986 provides the basis for the oil-for-food deal, and U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan has said he expects the Security Council to renew the oil sale agreement before June. Iraq is lobbying for $4 billion in oil sales, double its previous limit.
Russia, a major buyer of oil under the plan, is also anxious to extend cooperation with Iraq in oil development projects.
Moscow has been stepping up efforts to improve ties in Asia and the Middle East, partly as a counterbalance to NATO plans to admit new members in eastern Europe.
The Kremlin, which is equally interested in developing relations with prosperous Gulf states, also used the opportunity to lobby for Kuwait's interests.
"The Russian side encouraged (Iraq) to continue efforts to settle the problems concerning the fate of the missing Kuwaiti citizens and the return of Kuwaiti property," the statement said.
